covers.quote: Some conjunctions come in pairs, such as ‘whether/or’, 'both/and', ‘either/or’ and ‘neither/nor’.

examples.note: Both conjunctions are followed by adjectives.

parts.quote: Whether wet or dry, the weather won't stop us going ahead with the team-building exercise.

examples.note: Both conjunctions are followed by noun phrases.

parts.quote: My manager and I discussed both my performance review and my career prospects.

examples.note: Both conjunctions are followed by clauses.

parts.quote: Either we complete the report today, or we work on it tomorrow.

rules.quote: Each conjunction in the pair should appear before the same type of word, phrase or clause.
rules.violation_condition: a paired conjunction (correlative conjunction) where each element of the pair is followed by different grammatical structures (e.g. one followed by a noun phrase and the other by a clause)
when: When using paired (correlative) conjunctions such as 'whether/or', 'both/and', 'either/or', or 'neither/nor'.
rules.why: G-4: Marks the instruction sentence on parallel structure with correlative conjunctions; absorbs the heading and intro.

examples.note: Split into two sentences rather than joining with 'with'.

parts.quote: The lake has had several blue-green algae outbreaks this year. It has been closed to swimming at least once a year since 2002.

examples.note: Uses 'with' to attach an additional clause at the end of the sentence.

parts.quote: The lake has had several blue-green algae outbreaks this year, with the lake closed to swimming at least once a year since 2002.

rules.quote: Don’t use ‘with’ to add a clause at the beginning or end of a sentence.
rules.violation_condition: using 'with' to introduce an absolute clause or pseudo-conjunction clause at the beginning or end of a sentence
